activities.anchor: awards each district to whoever gets the most votes
activities.caption: mark the UK's typical disproportionality score
activities.name: vsGallagherPlace

config.prompt: The UK's typical Gallagher disproportionality index runs near which value?
config.why: Above 20 — against low single digits for the most proportional systems: the measurable gap between vote shares and seat shares.

activities.caption: bet on what 'most votes' actually means
activities.name: vsPluralityPredict

config.q: Under plurality with three or more candidates, does 'won the most votes' mean most voters wanted that winner?
choices: yes — most votes and majority support are the same claim
no — the winner can be the active second choice of most of the electorate
config.why: Plurality requires no majority — which is why majoritarian systems manufacture the majority that plurality merely presumes.

activities.caption: file each system feature under its family
activities.name: vsPRSort

config.prompt: Proportional versus majoritarian — file each feature:

items.label: party-list PR: seats match vote shares
STV: surplus votes transfer at a fractional value, per the Droop quota
MMP: constituency members topped up by list members to proportionality
Germany's 5% threshold keeps extremists and splinters out
IRV and two-round runoffs manufacture majority legitimacy in single-member seats

config.why: Coalitions are normal on the proportional side — governance by negotiation; the majoritarian fixes kill simple spoilers while paradoxes move rather than die.

activities.caption: drag the divider — two kinds of stability
activities.name: vsStabilityCompare

config.prompt: Drag the divider — what each system's stability actually is:

before.label: FPTP's kind
before.text: Decisive single-party government purchased with disproportional translation — landslides on a minority of votes, parties governing alone on a third of the electorate.

after.label: PR's kind
after.text: Germany, New Zealand and the Nordics are among the world's most stable and best-governed — coalition governance by negotiation.

config.why: What the system buys is not stability per se but a particular kind of stability — decisive single-party government.

activities.anchor: A referendum asks voters to decide an issue directly
activities.caption: walk the referendum-design decisions in order
activities.name: vsReferendumBranch

config.root: You are designing a referendum on a constitutional question. Walk the design calls.

start.text: First call: what goes to the voters directly, and what stays with representatives?

choices.label: Everything — one binary lever on the whole question
Constitutional identity and cross-cutting moral questions; amendable policy stays with representatives

binary.text: Binary framing compresses multi-dimensional questions into one lever — sovereignty, migration, economics and identity in one X: the Brexit problem. Campaigns reward emotional framing over deliberation.

scope.text: The constructive split: constitutional identity questions and moral cross-cutting issues suit voters; what needs deliberation and amendment suits representatives.

thresholds.text: Constitutional change on a 51-49 split of 40% turnout is a fragile mandate — and minority rights need safeguards, since courts may void referendums that violate rights.

choices.label: Last call: the question paper itself

wording.text: Wording effects are measurable and, on close votes, decisive — double negatives and framing shift support. The interface between voter and question is the last centimetre of design.

config.why: Referendums suit constitutional and cross-cutting moral questions — but binary framing, thresholds and wording are engineered risks, not accidents.

activities.anchor: Analysis means scoring systems against explicit criteria
activities.caption: one line of this gerrymandering briefing is wrong
activities.name: vsGerrySpot

config.prompt: One line of this student's briefing on detecting gerrymandering is wrong — click it:
lines: The efficiency gap measures wasted-vote asymmetry — votes piled up in lost districts and safe wins.
Ensemble methods simulate thousands of neutral districting plans and ask whether the actual map is an outlier.
A district's weird salamander shape is the reliable detector of gerrymandering.
Pennsylvania 2012: roughly half the statewide vote, five of eighteen seats — no neutral ensemble would plausibly produce that.
The offence is in the outcomes, not the outline.
config.correction: Shape is the folk detector and a poor one — natural geography contorts districts too, and a compact map can still be rigged; the modern detection is statistical.
config.why: Drawing district lines to predetermine outcomes is as old as the word — Elbridge Gerry's 1812 salamander — but the modern detection is wasted-vote asymmetry and ensembles.

config.prompt: What does turnout run at in compulsory-voting Australia?
config.why: Near 90% since 1924, versus voluntary systems' 50–65% — and the composition effects are the point: who turns out decides elections, so every turnout rule is a distributional choice about whose preferences count.

activities.anchor: The systems logic extends all the way to the paper
activities.caption: rebuild the butterfly-ballot failure chain
activities.name: vsButterflyOrder

config.prompt: Florida 2000, hole by hole — assemble the chain:
items: Palm Beach County's two-column butterfly ballot puts holes for adjacent entries
Tens of thousands of voters mispunch
Patrick Buchanan's tally runs roughly 3,000 votes above his plausible ceiling in a heavily Democratic county
The election is decided nationally by 537 votes
config.why: Ballot design is not decoration; on close margins it is the outcome — every interface between voter and count is a parameter, and each parameter is a potential kingmaker.
